Modality
Tags: courses,programs,specializations
Short Description: Identifies how a curricular offering is delivered, including in-person, online, or a combination of in-person and online instruction.
Modality
Modality identifies the method of delivery for a curricular offering, including courses, programs, and specializations. It describes whether instruction occurs in person, online, or through a combination of in-person and online instruction.
The University recognizes the following modalities:

In Person
Instruction occurs at a specified physical location on specified days and times. Less than 25% of instruction is delivered online.
In Person & Online Asynchronous
Instruction combines in-person meetings on specified days and times with online asynchronous instruction. The schedule of instruction and weekly time commitment for online asynchronous instruction must be clear to students in the syllabus on the first day of class. Neither modality may account for less than 25% of total instructional time.
In Person & Online Synchronous
Instruction combines in-person and online meetings on specified days and times. Neither modality may account for less than 25% of total instructional time.

Online Synchronous
All instruction occurs online at specified days and times.
Online Synchronous & Asynchronous
All instruction occurs online and combines synchronous meetings on specified days and times with asynchronous instruction. The schedule of instruction and weekly time commitment for online asynchronous instruction must be clear to students in the syllabus. Neither modality may account for less than 25% of total instructional time.
Online Asynchronous
All instruction occurs online with no required synchronous meetings at specified days and times, except for optional online office hours or meetings. The weekly time commitment for online asynchronous instruction must be clear to students in the syllabus.
See University Manual 8.30.30

Topics Course
Tags: courses
Short Description: A course that allows different topics to be offered under the same course number.
Topics Course
Topics courses allow different topics to be offered under the same course number.
8.81.20 Open-ended Course. An Open-ended Course shall be administered by the department which originated it. Initially, an open-ended course shall be proposed and approved in the same manner as other permanent courses (8.81.10). Prior to offering a specific topic the content of the course shall be approved in a department meeting.
8.81.21 After approval of each offering of an open-ended course topic, a copy of the title, subtitle, and description shall be forwarded for schedule authorization to the Office of Enrollment Services via the dean of the college in which the department resides. The dean’s authorization shall ensure that no overlap exists between specific topics and existing courses.

8.81.22 A specific topic within an open-ended course may be offered three times. After three offerings the topic shall be approved through the appropriate channels as either a permanent course or as a permanent topic within an open-ended course and shall be included in the University Catalog.

Short Description: A grading method in which student performance is recorded as S (Satisfactory) or U (Unsatisfactory) rather than a letter grade.
S/U Only

Certain courses do not lend themselves to precise grading. For these courses, only S (satisfactory) or U (unsatisfactory) is given to all students enrolled. S/U courses are labeled as such in the course descriptions in this catalog. S/U courses are not counted as courses taken under the Pass-Fail option.
D1 is the only General Education outcome that can be graded using S/U or Letter Grades. All other outcomes must be graded by Letter Grades.

Instructional Delivery Method
Tags: courses
Short Description: The instructional delivery method. Also known as "method of instruction.”
Instructional Delivery Method
Provided below is the complete list of approved methods of instruction, as proposed in FSEC Report #2024-2025-03 and subsequently approved by the Faculty Senate through Bill #24-25-12 on January 23, 2025.
A course in which the primary method is presentation and students are expected to participate in a variety of ways, such as small-group discussions, questions and answers, writing-exercises, etc.
Applied course work, generally involving experimentation or observation, typically using special equipment (including computers and specialized software).
Separate sections of a lecture course regularly scheduled for discussion.
Supervised work with an emphasis on performance and creativity in which faculty instruct, assist, and critique.
Course offered to a small group (usually no more than 20 students) where participants actively exchange ideas and findings based on readings or research.

One-on-one instruction in which the student enters into an agreement with the instructor that defines the focus of inquiry and nature of activities. Includes tutorials, directed readings, special projects.
Structured experiences where the primary aim is to connect theory with practice. Includes clinics, internships, externships, student teaching, field experiences. May include regular class meetings.
Similar to a seminar, with emphasis on applied rather than theoretical learning, but not offered for degree-program credit.
